Q: How do you read a lambda function as a string? A:

I propose the following:

import inspect
import dis
import ast
from typing import Callable
def get_lambda_source(f: Callable)->str:
    l: list[tuple[int, int]] = []
    for i in dis.get_instructions(f):
        p = i.positions
        q = p.lineno, p.col_offset
        r = p.end_lineno, p.end_col_offset
        if q != r:  # some classes
            l += q, r
    q, r = min(l), max(l)
    best = None
    class Finder(ast.NodeVisitor):
        def visit_Lambda(self, node: ast.Lambda):
            nonlocal best
            if (node.lineno, node.col_offset) < q <= r <= (node.end_lineno, node.end_col_offset):
                best = node.lineno, node.col_offset, node.end_lineno, node.end_col_offset
            self.generic_visit(node)
    sourcelines: list[str] = inspect.findsource(f)[0]
    Finder().visit(ast.parse(''.join(sourcelines)))
    line1, col1, line2, col2 = best
    if line1==line2:
        return sourcelines[line1-1][col1:col2]
    else:
        return ''.join([sourcelines[line1-1][col1:], *sourcelines[line1:line2-1], sourcelines[line2-1][:col2]])

Explanation: it uses dis module to disassemble the function, access .positions.{lineno,col_offset,end_lineno,end_col_offset}, then ast.parse the whole file and find the deepest lambda node that contains the range.

This relies on the following experimentally-observed behaviors:

  • the computed range (p,q) contains everything after the : (excluding redundant parentheses wrapping the whole expression)
  • the q != r check is to filter out some instructions that have col_offset=end_col_offset=0 for some reason.

It works even with nested lambdas:

In [2]: get_lambda_source([lambda: 1, lambda: 2][0])
Out[2]: 'lambda: 1'

In [3]: get_lambda_source([lambda: 1, lambda: 2][1])
Out[3]: 'lambda: 2'

In [4]: f = ("""
   ...:         """, lambda:3)[1]

In [5]: get_lambda_source(f)
Out[5]: 'lambda:3'

In [6]: f = lambda x=lambda:lambda:None:lambda:x

In [7]: get_lambda_source(f)
Out[7]: 'lambda x=lambda:lambda:None:lambda:x'

In [8]: get_lambda_source(f())
Out[8]: 'lambda:x'

In [9]: get_lambda_source(f()())
Out[9]: 'lambda:lambda:None'

In [10]: get_lambda_source(f()()())
Out[10]: 'lambda:None'

In [13]: f = lambda:((((
    ...:     123
    ...:     ))))
    ...: get_lambda_source(f)
Out[13]: 'lambda:((((\n    123\n    ))))'

It looks rather ugly, but the built-in inspect module isn't much better, containing things like:

    if ismethod(object):
        object = object.__func__
    if isfunction(object):
        object = object.__code__
    if istraceback(object):
        object = object.tb_frame
    if isframe(object):
        object = object.f_code

This can be slow though (disassemble the whole file just for the lambda). On the positive side,

  • you can cache the ast.parse output, so you only need to parse each file once.
  • the example with """ before the lambda above causes an error when inspect.getsource is used, but not with the proposal above.

In [12]: f = ("""
    ...:         """, lambda:3)[1]
    ...: inspect.getsource(f)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TokenError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
...
TokenError: ('EOF in multi-line string', (1, 9))

Q: What is the difference between typedef struct {} Node and typedef struct _node{} Node in C? A:

In the first case you have a new type that maps to an anonymous named structure, in the second case you can use both struct _node and Node as indistinguishable types. In the first case you can use that type only (Node). The anonymous struct will be usable only in the definition.
